sections.heading: 1. Assign twelve plays to accountable seats, not twelve miniature businesses
paragraphs: Treat the twelve mapped operator plays as one controlled inventory business with three operating lanes. For this chapter's staffing map, label them P01 multi-exchange broadcasting, P02 exchange spread capture, P03 event drop-curve repricing, P04 NFL playoff strips, P05 NBA playoff strips, P06 SSL-linked playoff options, P07 suite seat-splitting, P08 suite group placements, P09 Super Bowl hospitality, P10 World Cup hospitality, P11 F1 hospitality, and P12 permissioned sponsor-allotment bundles for Masters or Final Four demand. These labels allocate work; they do not assert that every rights holder permits resale or every ticket includes hospitality access. The owner underwrites acquisition, signs supplier contracts, approves event exposure, and owns cash forecasting. Contractor C1 operates listings, pricing rules, and transfer exceptions. Contractor C2 handles corporate proposals, suite guest manifests, supplier confirmations, and invoice matching. Both contractors work against documented deliverables rather than sharing an unrestricted administrator account. The owner remains the escalation seat when either specialist is unavailable. Maintain one inventory identifier across the purchase document, POS record, exchange order, barcode transfer, and accounting cohort. Every play must inherit these controls before its first listing, including a backup contact who can halt sales without needing the owner's personal device.

Separate the capital and settlement profiles before assigning workload. Multi-exchange resale uses SkyBox, Automatiq, or Logitix as the selected system of record, with verified integrations to StubHub, Vivid Seats, SeatGeek, and TickPick; integration coverage and synchronization latency must be tested rather than assumed. Inventory is commonly purchased before sale, and an exchange may release proceeds only after the event under its seller agreement. Suite splitting adds a fixed suite commitment, per-seat occupancy risk, catering minimums, parking entitlements, and a hard guest-manifest deadline. A partially sold suite can generate cash receipts while remaining economically underwater. Tentpole hospitality adds supplier deposits, staged corporate collections, hotel or transport deliverables, and refund mismatches across multiple providers. Super Bowl, World Cup, and F1 packages therefore need component-level obligations, not merely ticket quantities. Never treat a sponsor allocation as freely transferable because a contact offered it informally. Confirm the supplier's authority and each component's resale restrictions before taking customer money. For all three lanes, measure time from acquisition cash leaving the bank until unrestricted settlement arrives. A profitable event with a delayed payout can exhaust the same working capital needed to fulfill the following week's contracted orders.

Expand to the five-person pod only when an eight-week workload record shows sustained exceptions or corporate fulfillment exceeding existing capacity, and settled contribution funds the added seat. The second full-time employee becomes operations lead, owning daily exception triage, event readiness, and contractor quality assurance. C1 remains the exchange execution specialist; C2 remains hospitality fulfillment; C3 supplies reconciliation and reporting deliverables. The owner retains capital allocation and senior corporate relationships but should no longer be the only person who can explain an event's margin. Write a responsibility matrix separating purchase authority, listing authority, refund authority, and bank-payment release. Require two-person evidence review for supplier bank-detail changes without giving every worker banking access. Contractor status follows actual working conditions, not the letter C in a staffing model: evaluate federal employment standards, tax classification, and applicable state tests before imposing employee-like schedules or control. Use contracted event coverage windows and service outcomes where genuine independence exists. If classification requires payroll employment, reprice the operating plan rather than hiding payroll costs inside a nominal contractor budget. The scorecard's team counts describe capacity assumptions, not permission to misclassify the people who perform the work.

callout.title: Make institutional knowledge survive the owner's absence
callout.body: A buyer values evidence that another qualified operator can reproduce the spread without borrowing the founder's personal credentials.
items: Record each suite's actual seating configuration, obstructed positions, catering minimums, parking allocation, and guest cutoff before splitting inventory.
Keep a permissioned event-day supplier roster with alternate contacts; test the alternate before Super Bowl or World Cup travel begins.

Run a supervised owner-absence event cycle and record every escalation that still requires personal relationships or undocumented knowledge.

sections.heading: 2. Pay for settled quality and review a scorecard that exposes hidden losses
paragraphs: Contractor compensation should purchase reliable execution, not encourage inventory churn. For the Base pod, an illustrative monthly contract could pay C1 a $1,200 service retainer and C2 a $1,000 service retainer for explicitly bounded deliverables. Add a combined variable pool of up to 3% of positive event contribution after acquisition, exchange fees, markdowns, customer remedies, and event-specific fulfillment costs, but before the pool itself. Specify this ordering in the contract so the calculation cannot become circular. Pay the variable component after settlement reconciliation and a documented claims review, with a final true-up under agreed terms. These figures illustrate contract design, not additional profit on top of the canonical case; retainers, incentives, replacement coverage, and employer costs where applicable must fit inside its expense allowance. Do not impose arbitrary wage deductions or pass every exchange penalty directly to a worker. Assign errors by evidence, distinguish platform outages from controllable mistakes, and define commercially reasonable remediation. A contractor who flags a cancellation risk early should not lose the same quality score as one who conceals it. Separate speed, accuracy, and economic outcomes so a fast transfer cannot disguise an unprofitable purchase or an unresolved customer complaint.

Hold a thirty-minute weekly operating review using the same event-cohort export every time. Start with unrestricted cash, committed acquisitions, customer refund obligations, and expected post-event exchange receipts; then examine contribution and service quality. Set an internal target of zero duplicate fills and 100% evidence-backed transfer completion by contractual deadlines. For active event windows, contract an exception acknowledgment target such as fifteen minutes, with named backup coverage and an earlier internal transfer deadline than the exchange requires. These are negotiated service targets, not claims about vendor uptime. Track synchronization acknowledgment age and stop affected listings whenever their state cannot be verified. A POS auto-hold must demonstrably propagate across enabled exchanges; a local screen showing sold is insufficient. Model the cited 200% replacement-penalty exposure as a stress case wherever relevant contractual terms support it, rather than assuming every marketplace uses an identical penalty. Review unsold units by days to event, realized versus underwritten spread, postponement reserve coverage, and payout days past contractual expectation. Give each breach an owner, a cash impact, and a dated correction. Never accept ticket count or gross billings as a substitute for these operating measurements.

Concentration discipline belongs in the weekly scorecard, not only the eventual sale presentation. Cap each corporate customer and each acquisition counterparty at 25% of trailing-twelve-month retained contribution and at 25% of forward committed acquisition exposure, using separate denominators for the two tests. Aggregate related entities and commonly controlled purchasing accounts. Also cap each exchange at 25% of unsettled receivables when the available channel mix permits that policy; if it does not, reduce commitments rather than labeling the risk diversified. Launch cohorts with tiny denominators will naturally fail percentage tests, so identify them explicitly as concentrated and stop increasing the dominant exposure until the book broadens. A buyer should see that history, not a retrospective rewrite. All-in pricing checks belong beside transfer accuracy: 16 CFR Part 464 addresses live-event ticket price presentation, while New York Article 25 adds jurisdiction-specific reseller requirements. The BOTS Act, 15 U.S.C. 45c, prohibits covered security-measure circumvention and certain sales involving tickets obtained that way. Contractors must use permitted inventory sources and approved integrations, never queue-bypass automation. Preserve acquisition provenance and listing price evidence so operational quality remains auditable after a contractor leaves or an exchange disputes fulfillment.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile gross billings, retained contribution and event-cohort cash
paragraphs: Use the Formula v2.0 retained-share bridge without confusing ticket transaction value with operator economics. Conservative gross operating billings of $220,000 less $132,000 of ticket and suite acquisition produce $88,000 retained contribution at 40%. Subtract $61,600 of remaining costs to reach $26,400 owner profit: 12% of gross billings and 30% of retained contribution. Base billings of $1,010,000 less $606,000 acquisition produce $404,000 retained contribution; $212,100 of remaining costs leave $191,900, or 19.0% gross and 47.5% retained margin. Scaled billings of $1,800,000 less $1,080,000 acquisition produce $720,000 retained contribution; $252,000 remaining costs leave $468,000, or 26% gross and 65% retained margin. Remaining costs must include exchange sell fees, unsold inventory and markdown slippage, expected cancellation or postponement clawback losses, labor, software, fulfillment, and financing charges where incurred. Do not deduct acquisition twice. Do not count hotel or venue transaction values outside the operator's contracted billings. These are exact annual planning reconciliations; the expense residuals are constraints to substantiate with detailed budgets, not evidence that any particular staffing contract automatically achieves the stated margin. A cost overrun changes forecast profit rather than disappearing inside the fixed 40% retained-share assumption.

Build an event subledger that separates recognition from collection. Record customer deposits against unperformed obligations, supplier advances against undelivered components, ticket inventory where appropriate, and exchange receivables according to the actual contractual rights. Recognize revenue when the relevant performance obligation is satisfied under the adopted accounting policy, not simply when a buyer pays or an event date passes. Ticket-only delivery and a hosted hospitality package may have different fulfillment patterns. Assess principal-versus-agent presentation under ASC 606 for each arrangement: control before transfer, responsibility for fulfillment, inventory risk, and pricing discretion require documented judgment. The scorecard's 40% retained contribution is an analytical net basis, not a universal instruction to report exactly 40% as financial-statement revenue. A principal arrangement may report gross revenue and acquisition cost separately; an agent arrangement reports its fee or commission. Maintain a bridge from either presentation to the canonical scorecard. When an exchange remits cash net of sell fees, reconstruct the gross settlement and record the fee once. Otherwise a bookkeeper can both understate billings and deduct the same fee again, creating a false explanation for an event's apparently weak retained margin.

Close cohorts by event, purchase batch, channel, and package component, retaining both underwriting and actual outcomes. Treat a markdown as reduced realized proceeds or an explicitly bridged planning variance, never both. Unsold expired inventory requires the appropriate write-down; recoverable postponed inventory needs a supported recoverability assessment rather than an automatic full loss. Distinguish expected clawback expense and related obligations from a management cash reserve: earmarking cash does not itself create another expense. Post-event payout delay affects liquidity and any actual financing cost, while a doubtful receivable requires a separate collection assessment. Maintain a rolling thirteen-week cash forecast and stress a thirty-day settlement delay alongside simultaneous event postponements. The stated $10,000-$50,000 startup capital range does not automatically finance the Scaled case's acquisition pipeline. Fund timing gaps through retained cash, genuine supplier terms, or appropriately priced facilities and include their charges in forecasts. Monthly operating overhead within the $1,800-$11,000 planning range excludes the separate inventory funding requirement. A buyer should be able to trace a single Super Bowl package from signed scope through supplier payment, customer delivery, final settlement, and the remaining refund exposure without asking the owner to reconstruct it orally.

sections.heading: 4. Price transferable earnings, document ownership and preserve the cash-cow option
paragraphs: Build the transfer file before asking anyone to pay a premium. Obtain signed confidentiality terms, a present assignment of commissioned copyright interests, and delivery of editable source materials from each contractor. Under 17 U.S.C. 204(a), a copyright ownership transfer generally requires a signed writing from the owner or an authorized agent. Do not rely exclusively on a work-for-hire label for contractor-created software, pricing scripts, or operating manuals. Identify pre-existing contractor tools and secure adequate licenses for anything embedded in the deliverable. Copyright ownership does not itself transfer exchange accounts, customer permissions, supplier contracts, or venue entitlements. List assignment and change-of-control provisions separately, then obtain required counterparties' written permissions. Use business-controlled email, role-based access, documented recovery procedures, and individual credentials; transfer administration through permitted platform procedures rather than sharing passwords. Retain corporate purchasing histories only within the applicable contractual and privacy permissions. A clean data room includes event-cohort statements, bank reconciliations, tax filings, rights provenance, contractor agreements, incident history, and customer renewal evidence. It also records what cannot transfer. A buyer discounts unassignable access and personal favors even when those relationships generated excellent historical ticket spreads.

Value the operation on normalized transferable earnings rather than gross ticket billings. For preliminary small-business underwriting, use an explicitly illustrative 2.0-3.0 times normalized seller's discretionary earnings for an owner-operated book and 3.0-4.0 times normalized EBITDA for a genuinely manager-run business. These are negotiation sensitivities, not observed transaction comparables or an automatic premium for using a POS. Before applying them, reconcile owner profit to the selected earnings definition, adding back only evidenced eligible items and preserving recurring labor, claims, and replacement costs. If Base owner profit of $191,900 is treated as an SDE proxy with no further adjustments, the illustrative enterprise-value range is $383,800-$575,700. If an absentee buyer must spend an additional $90,000 annually on fully loaded replacement management, the simplified earnings proxy becomes $101,900; at 3.0-4.0 times, the range is $305,700-$407,600. This proxy is not audited EBITDA without the full reconciliation. Apply replacement expense only for duties not already funded in the pod. Strong margins do not justify counting the same manager twice or pretending the founder's sales work has no economic cost.

Negotiate price, working capital, and contingent risk as separate schedules. Enterprise value is not closing cash: debt, agreed cash treatment, normal working capital, transaction expenses, escrows, and contingent consideration change proceeds. Define whether ticket inventory, supplier advances, exchange receivables, customer deposits, and refund obligations enter the working-capital calculation. Prevent deposits from appearing as free seller cash while the buyer inherits all fulfillment costs. Set any earnout against precisely defined settled cohort contribution, with rules for cancellation losses, channel migration, related-party sales, and buyer-controlled marketing spend. A headline multiple inflated by an uncertain earnout may deliver less value than a lower cash offer. The premium case rests on diversified repeat corporate demand, transferable supplier rights, low founder dependence, clean claims history, and reproducible settlement records. If those conditions do not support an attractive offer, retain the cash-cow structure: distribute only cash above event commitments, tax obligations, expected remedies, and the stress liquidity buffer. Compare holding the business with sale proceeds after taxes and transition workload, not with a promotional multiple. Revisit the decision after each full event season using actual owner hours and cash distributions.

chapters.question_prompt: What is the exact Day-1-to-Day-30 execution schedule for launching live-event, super bowl & vip ticket brokering, and what quantitative thresholds govern Kill, Fix, or Scale decisions at Day 30/60/90?
chapters.title: The First 30-Day Launch Sprint & Kill / Fix / Scale Gates
chapters.subtitle: A Three-Person SkyBox, Automatiq, and Logitix Launch Plan with BOTS Act Controls, Suite Rights Verification, and Settlement-Adjusted Capital Tests
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #43 ranks #02 of 43 with a 95/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. This sprint maps 12 operator plays across multi-exchange resale, stadium suite seat-splitting, and tentpole corporate hospitality, but funds only one initial lane. One full-time owner and two contractors establish transfer rights, test inventory locks, secure buyer demand, and reconcile cash before expanding exposure. Canonical annual owner profits are $26,400 Conservative, $191,900 Base, and $468,000 Scaled; none is a 30-day sales target. Daily deliverables culminate in quantitative Day 30/60/90 Kill, Fix, or Scale decisions based on completed orders, realized margin, settlement aging, and stressed liquidity. A $3,000 first-month overhead ceiling protects capital while the normal one-to-three-month first-deal window unfolds.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1-7: Define the Twelve Plays, Lock Rights, and Ring-Fence Cash
paragraphs: Day 1 starts with a bounded operating map, not twelve simultaneous launches. For this chapter, the twelve mapped plays are P01 authorized multi-exchange ticket resale; P02 contractual sponsor-allotment resale; P03 NFL playoff-option strips; P04 NBA playoff-option strips; P05 full-suite seat-splitting; P06 weekday suite corporate seat blocks; P07 Super Bowl hospitality bundles; P08 World Cup hospitality bundles; P09 F1 hospitality bundles; P10 Masters hospitality bundles; P11 Final Four hospitality bundles; and P12 repeat corporate hospitality procurement. These are operating workstreams within Candidate #43, not twelve independent profit forecasts. P01-P04 carry ticket acquisition and exchange settlement exposure; P05-P06 concentrate capital in a suite whose unsold seats expire together; P07-P12 add supplier deposits, package obligations, and corporate collection timing. Score each against transferable inventory, verified buyer demand, cash duration, and replacement exposure. Choose one funded pilot and one unfunded backup. Favor nearby events with inspectable supply and published payout terms rather than a distant tentpole that consumes the entire launch reserve. The owner handles purchasing, contracts, and exceptions; contractor A handles listings and transfer evidence; contractor B handles buyer outreach and reconciliation. Reserve forty owner hours and ten hours per contractor weekly, with event-day coverage scheduled explicitly.

Use a $25,000 illustrative launch bankroll inside the canonical $10,000-$50,000 startup range. Allocate $10,000 to acquisition exposure, $7,500 to a protected refund and replacement reserve, $3,000 to first-month overhead, and $4,500 to uncommitted cash. Cap cumulative overhead at $750 on Day 7, $1,500 on Day 14, $2,250 on Day 21, and $3,000 on Day 30. The illustrative monthly budget assigns $1,200 to contractor coverage, $1,200 to software and integration access, $300 to insurance and accounting, and $300 to outbound activity. Obtain actual quotations before committing; if a suitable vendor exceeds its allowance, reduce scope rather than silently increasing burn. Acquisition payments are tracked separately from overhead but still consume bank cash. Owner draws reduce available capital and cannot disappear from the liquidity test. A $10,000 launch must shrink inventory exposure, not borrow the protected reserve to imitate this allocation. Do not buy a whole suite merely because its seat-level spread looks attractive. Its deposit, catering minimum, and unsold-seat risk can exceed the bankroll before a single customer settles. Keep all reserves liquid and exclude unsettled exchange receivables from immediately available cash.

Days 2-7 establish enforceable supply and observable inventory behavior. For every proposed purchase, record seller identity, original order evidence, section and row, delivery deadline, transfer restrictions, event status, and cancellation treatment. A suite agreement must expressly permit the intended seat distribution and identify food, alcohol, parking, and admission entitlements. Hospitality components require separate supplier confirmation; possessing an event ticket does not establish authorization to resell an official package. Map purchaser and event jurisdictions before listing. Apply 15 U.S.C. §45c to acquisition methods: prohibit queue bypass, purchase-limit circumvention, and security-measure evasion. Review New York Arts and Cultural Affairs Law Article 25 where applicable, including reseller licensing and ticket-price disclosures. Apply 16 CFR Part 464 to covered live-event price presentations, including mandatory package charges. Evaluate SkyBox, Automatiq, or Logitix against documented marketplace support rather than assumed universal connectivity. Test StubHub, Vivid Seats, SeatGeek, and TickPick individually when available under the actual account agreement. A local auto-hold is necessary but cannot prove instantaneous remote withdrawal. Log acknowledgments and suspend any connector with unbounded lag. Where a test environment is unavailable, use vendor-supervised validation or one controlled real listing; never manufacture customer purchases to generate test activity.

callout.title: Four Pre-Flight Checks Before the First Purchase
callout.body: Release acquisition cash only after the owner can produce the evidence below for the exact pilot inventory.
items: Rights: Match the seller's authority, event restrictions, suite distribution permissions, and promised delivery date to the buyer-facing offer.
Inventory: Complete twenty connector tests, require local holds within two seconds and remote acknowledgments within sixty seconds, and disable any failing channel.
Cash: Preserve the greater of $7,500 or modeled stressed obligations, plus the next thirty days of committed overhead; do not count exchange receivables as bank cash.
Pricing: Display applicable mandatory charges upfront, document supplier and exchange deductions, and confirm that acquisition methods satisfy 15 U.S.C. §45c.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8-14: Build Contribution Ledgers and Run One Controlled Pilot
paragraphs: Days 8-10 build the ledger before the sales dashboard. Preserve the scorecard's exact annual relationships: Conservative gross fee basis of $220,000 less $132,000 acquisition cost produces $88,000 retained revenue; subtracting $61,600 of remaining costs produces $26,400 owner profit. Base uses $1,010,000 less $606,000 acquisition cost, leaving $404,000 retained revenue; $212,100 of remaining costs leaves $191,900 profit. Scaled uses $1,800,000 less $1,080,000 acquisition cost, leaving $720,000 retained revenue; $252,000 of remaining costs leaves $468,000 profit. These reconcile to gross-basis margins of 12%, 19.0%, and 26%, and retained margins of 30%, 47.5%, and 65%. Remaining costs must include exchange selling fees, inventory markdowns and write-offs, postponement or cancellation reserves, payment costs, carrying costs, and operating overhead. The 40% retained share is the supplied net-contribution model, not a declaration that every contract receives identical ASC 606 presentation. Determine principal-versus-agent treatment from actual control and contractual responsibilities. Never label the underlying event economy or corporate entertainment budget as operator revenue. Store gross customer consideration, channel fees, and net remittance separately. If an imported exchange payout already deducts a fee, reconstruct the bridge before applying the scorecard; do not deduct that fee twice.

Keep the three operating lanes economically separate even when their headline retained share matches. A multi-exchange example starts with $1,000 customer consideration and $600 acquisition cost. Deduct $100 selling fees, $50 inventory slippage, $25 cancellation reserve, $10 carrying cost, and $50 allocated overhead: owner contribution is $165, not the $400 acquisition spread. A suite example sells eight seats for $1,250 each against a $6,000 suite commitment. Deduct $200 payment costs, $600 catering obligations, $500 markdown allowance, $300 cancellation reserve, $100 carrying cost, and $500 overhead; contribution is $1,800. The suite's entire acquisition commitment remains exposed if buyers disappear. A hospitality example bills $20,000 against $12,000 ticket and supplier acquisition cost, then deducts $600 payment costs, $1,000 service delivery, $800 slippage, $600 cancellation reserve, $200 carrying cost, and $1,000 overhead, leaving $3,800. These illustrative transactions explain mechanics; they do not replace the canonical annual scenarios. Separate supplier deposits, buyer deposits, event delivery, and final settlement dates. Corporate deposits can support procurement only within their contractual refund conditions. They are neither immediately earned profit nor unrestricted owner distributions. Exchange payouts arriving after the event create a different capital cycle from directly invoiced suite seats, even with identical accounting margin.

Days 11-14 run the smallest pilot that can validate the full chain. For P01, use transferable inventory with enough time to withdraw listings, complete delivery, and correct an exception before doors open. For P05-P06, require a signed suite agreement and a seat-level allocation register before accepting money. For P07-P12, quote only supplier-confirmed components and specify substitutions, delivery milestones, and cancellation treatment. Keep P03-P04 option exposure separate from delivered admissions: document what happens when a team fails to qualify, when a series ends early, or when an SSL agreement restricts resale. Contractor B records qualified opportunities and signed orders without counting either as settled sales. Contractor A records every listing change, purchase acknowledgment, hold, transfer, and buyer receipt. The owner approves acquisition and handles unresolved exceptions. Test a contractual replacement charge as high as 200% of the affected order where the actual channel terms support that exposure; do not assume every marketplace uses that formula. Combine unrelated-event replacement exposure with a canceled-event refund obligation and an unsold-inventory markdown shock. Avoid counting mutually exclusive remedies twice. If the protected reserve cannot absorb that stress, reduce inventory before pursuing another buyer, regardless of the apparent quoted margin.

Day 9: Owner verifies all three canonical annual scenarios.

callout.title: Four Habits That Protect Spread After the Sale
callout.body: Veteran operators optimize delivered contribution and cash duration, not the prettiest advertised markup.
items: Request the exchange's actual event-specific payout rule before purchasing; a high-spread ticket held through a distant event can produce poor cash turnover.
Photograph or archive the suite seating plan and entitlement schedule; distinguish fixed seats, standing access, catering minimums, and parking before splitting inventory.
Give each sponsor-allotment source a rights checklist and delivery deadline; relationship access does not itself establish transferable resale rights.
Record the last profitable exit price before buying an NFL or NBA playoff strip; revise qualification probabilities without allowing automated repricing to override contractual inventory limits.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15-21: Prove Fulfillment, Reconcile Payouts, and Measure Failure
paragraphs: Week three converts pipeline activity into auditable fulfillment evidence. On Day 15, contractor A checks each upcoming event against the ticketing system's transfer availability and the promised delivery deadline. A barcode image is not adequate proof of a valid transfer; retain the platform's recipient confirmation or another contractually accepted delivery record. Day 16 tests repricing with hard floors derived from acquisition cost, expected selling fees, remaining reserve needs, and the approved exit strategy. Do not let a generic dynamic drop curve sell suite seats below the remaining suite obligation without owner acknowledgment. Day 17 tests one disruption tabletop: postponement, cancellation, or supplier failure. Record who contacts the buyer, who freezes listings, and which contract determines refund timing. Day 18 reconciles the earliest available settlement, including withheld amounts and adjustments. If the event has not occurred or payout is not yet due, mark the order as open with its contractual maturity date; never manufacture completion to satisfy the sprint. Days 19-21 review buyer conversion, supplier delivery reliability, and event-level exposure. Keep acquisition decisions with the owner while contractors operate documented checklists. After-hours coverage must name a reachable primary and backup before any event-day inventory remains listed.

Build a compact daily scorecard with denominators that resist vanity metrics. A completed order requires delivered entitlements, an elapsed event where relevant, and reconciled settlement; retain an appropriate reserve for later contractual claims. Count distinct economically independent orders, not split invoices manufactured from one corporate buyer. Track delivered-on-time orders divided by delivered orders, duplicate fills per accepted order, realized contribution after inventory losses, and owner net margin after all pilot overhead. Measure payout aging from the contractually due date, not from the sale date. Report overdue balances as a share of all due settlement balances, and show absolute dollars alongside percentages. Reconciliation variance equals unexplained settlement differences divided by the expected amount due. Report open inventory at acquisition cost with a separate estimated liquidation value; charging a markdown allowance and later recording the same realized loss requires a reserve release to prevent double counting. Allocate shared overhead consistently across plays, while showing the unallocated launch total so weak plays cannot hide inside accounting choices. When no settlement is due, there is no aging observation; the evidence requirement remains unmet. Pipeline quotations, deposits, and transfer confirmations cannot substitute for demonstrated collection.

Use liquidity coverage to decide whether another sale is safe. Calculate available liquidity as unrestricted bank cash less the next thirty days of committed overhead. Exclude undelivered buyer deposits needed for refunds and do not add unsettled marketplace balances. For the stress denominator, estimate incremental cash needed for a 20% markdown on open unsold inventory, full buyer refunds for one affected event before supplier recovery, and the documented replacement remedy on the largest independent open order. Where a refund deposit has already been excluded from the numerator, exclude the matching funded refund amount from the denominator to avoid double reservation. Apply the actual agreement if its remedy exceeds the illustrative replacement shock. This is a planning stress, not a maximum-loss claim. Maintain the separate $7,500 baseline reserve in the illustrative bankroll even when the current modeled denominator is smaller. A zero-exposure ledger does not establish commercial readiness; collection and fulfillment evidence still control expansion. Track capital-days as cash committed multiplied by days until unrestricted recovery. This exposes why a Super Bowl package purchased months ahead may be less deployable than a smaller nearby resale. Release reserves only against documented extinguishment or reduction of the underlying obligations.

sections.heading: 4. Days 22-30 and Beyond: Apply Quantitative Kill, Fix, or Scale Decisions
paragraphs: Days 22-29 assemble a decision packet rather than chase last-minute volume. Reprice stale inventory, confirm remaining supplier commitments, reconcile each bank receipt, and classify every unresolved exception. Compare plays using realized net contribution and capital-days, not quoted spread. The owner conducts a loss review on every markdown, refund, and delivery failure; contractors bring timestamps and documents rather than recollections. On Day 26, rerun the cash stress with current event concentrations and actual contractual remedies. On Day 27, prepare a continuation budget funded only by genuinely available cash. Cumulative overhead ceilings are $3,000 at Day 30, $6,000 at Day 60, and $9,000 at Day 90. These are maximum authorizations, not instructions to spend: the initial $25,000 allocation cannot fund every extension without releasing inventory capital or generating completed contribution. Do not consume protected reserves to meet the calendar. Day 28 documents contractor capacity and coverage gaps. Day 29 freezes the reporting cutoff and distinguishes open events from completed cohorts. Because the canonical first-deal window is one to three months, a clean but immature pilot normally receives Fix with restricted spending, not an invented Scale result or an automatic commercial failure verdict.

At each checkpoint, apply safety stops first, evidence minimums second, and economic thresholds third. Kill the affected play immediately for fabricated supply, prohibited acquisition methods, an unresolved required license, or inability to fund obligations; stop new sales while fulfilling or refunding existing contracts. A double fill triggers an immediate channel freeze and incident review, even when the overall business remains viable. With adequate completed evidence, Kill thresholds are owner net margin at or below negative 10% on Day 30, negative 5% on Day 60, or zero on Day 90. Evidence minimums are ten independent completed orders across two events, twenty-five across four events, and fifty across six events respectively. Below those minimums, choose Fix without increasing capital; at Day 90, stop paid acquisition if there are no signed orders after sixty qualified buyer conversations and twenty written quotes. Scale requires all checkpoint conditions simultaneously, including net margins of at least 12%, 15%, and 19% respectively. Require at least 99% on-time delivery and zero double fills in the evaluation window. Between Kill and Scale lies Fix: assign one measurable defect, an owner, and a fourteen-day retest. No unresolved safety defect may be averaged away by stronger sales.

Scale is a controlled capital increment, not permission to activate all twelve plays. At Day 30, require liquidity coverage of at least 1.25 times the modeled stress, overdue settlement balances no greater than 5% of due balances, and unexplained reconciliation variance no greater than 1%. Day 60 tightens coverage to 1.50 times, overdue balances to 2%, and variance to 0.5%; Day 90 retains 1.50 times coverage while tightening overdue balances to 1% and retaining 0.5% variance. All checkpoints preserve the baseline reserve, funded overhead, and twenty-percent single-event capital cap. A passing checkpoint permits at most a 25% increase in acquisition exposure for the proven lane; add a second play only after that increment clears a complete settlement cycle. Keep the launch pod at one full-time owner and two contractors until documented exception volume justifies staffing expansion. The canonical Scaled case requires two full-time people plus three contractors, not the original three-person workload stretched indefinitely. Compare annual forecasts with the exact scorecard only after accounting for event seasonality, holiday concentration, and cash duration. A profitable Final Four weekend cannot simply be multiplied by fifty-two. Publish the decision, released capital, retained reserves, corrective actions, and next checkpoint in one dated operating memo.
